🚨 Most engineers spend years learning how systems work.
💡 The best engineers spend years learning how systems fail.
One of the biggest mindset shifts in Distributed Systems is realizing that failures are not rare events.
⚠️ They are inevitable.
At scale:
🖥️ Servers fail
🌐 Networks partition
📩 Messages get delayed
💾 Disks become slow
⏳ Dependencies time out
📈 Traffic spikes unexpectedly
The question is no longer:
❌ "Will the system fail?"
The real question is:
✅ "How gracefully will it fail?"
As systems scale, there are a few critical failure modes every engineer should understand.

🌐 1️⃣ Network Partitions
Imagine a distributed system suddenly splitting into isolated groups that can no longer communicate.
Each side believes:
✅ "I'm healthy"
✅ "My data is correct"
❌ Neither side knows what the other is doing.
This single challenge is one of the reasons distributed systems are so difficult to design.

🧠 2️⃣ Split-Brain Scenarios
Things get even more dangerous.
Both isolated clusters elect their own leader 👑
Both continue accepting writes ✍️
Both believe they are the source of truth 📖
When connectivity returns, you're not solving a networking problem anymore.
You're solving a data consistency nightmare 😬
💸 And data integrity problems are among the most expensive failures in software engineering.

❓3️⃣ Partial Failures
One of the most deceptive failure modes.
A client sends a request 📤
No response arrives 📭
What happened?
🤔 Did the request never arrive?
🤔 Did the server crash?
🤔 Did processing succeed but the response get lost?
🤔 Is the server still working?
The scary part?
👀 All four situations can look exactly the same to the client.
This is why concepts like:
🔄 Retries
⏰ Timeouts
🔑 Idempotency
📡 Distributed coordination
are so important.

🩶 4️⃣ Gray Failures
The failures that make engineers question reality.
📊 Dashboards look healthy.
✅ Health checks pass.
🟢 Monitoring shows green everywhere.
Yet...
😡 Users experience slow responses.
😡 Queries time out.
😡 Applications feel broken.
The system appears healthy on the outside but is struggling internally.
Examples:
💽 Slow disks
🗑️ Long GC pauses
🌐 Intermittent networking issues
⚙️ Resource starvation
These failures are notoriously difficult to detect.

🔁 5️⃣ Amplification Loops
Many major outages start from a tiny problem.
📈 Small latency increase
⬇️
🔄 Retries increase
⬇️
📊 Load increases
⬇️
⏳ Latency increases further
⬇️
💥 Outage


🌊 6️⃣ Cascading Failures
One node fails.
⬇️
Traffic shifts to healthy nodes.
⬇️
Those nodes become overloaded.
⬇️
More nodes fail.
⬇️
Even more traffic shifts.
⬇️
💥 Entire system impacted.

Your expenses are quietly getting heavier.

You won’t feel inflation when it starts. 
You’ll feel it when your normal life starts costing just a little more every month.

Same grocery list, slightly higher bill. 
Same Swiggy order, less comfort for the same spend. 
Same salary, a tighter month end.

Crisil data shows something important.
The WPI input-output ratio is 1.02 in April 2026.

For the first time in 44 months, input costs for companies are rising faster than output prices. 

In simple terms, companies are paying more to make products than what they can quickly recover from customers.

And it’s broad based.

Copper up 17.3%, aluminium 20.6%, crude-linked inputs 49.3%, gas 19.1%.

These sit inside everything
Phones, cars, groceries, packaging, electricity.

So prices don’t jump suddenly. They adjust slowly.
A small revision here. A quiet increase there.

Because demand is still strong, companies will pass some of this on.
Not loudly. Not suddenly. But steadily.

And that’s why inflation never feels like a shock. 
It feels like money just doesn’t stretch anymore.

Where are you noticing this first in your own monthly spending?

Pastillas para no soñar

En Colombia hace rato nos tomamos pastillas para no soñar. Faltan cuatro días para elecciones y, otra vez, ningún candidato de los que puntea me genera esperanza. Seriamente. Hace muchos años que ninguno.

No es desidia. Es que ya ni siquiera espero. Vamos elección tras elección eligiendo personalidades rimbombantes, el que grita más fuerte, el que insulta mejor, el que promete con más cara dura. 

Nos enamoramos del estruendo. Del personaje. Del que se siente fuerte cuando todo se siente frágil.

De fondo, una pastilla. Para no imaginarnos un país distinto. Para no tener que soñar con coaliciones raras, con tipos aburridos pero serios, con gente que cambia de opinión cuando le muestran datos. Soñar duele. Es más fácil escoger el bando y gritarle al otro.

¿En qué momento empezamos a confundir carácter con quien grita de forma más elocuente? ¿En qué momento dejamos de querer presidentes y empezamos a querer protagonistas?

Carácter no es ruido, es lo contrario.

Las democracias que sobrevivieron a momentos así no lo hicieron por mesías. 

Lo hicieron por gente común que se negó a tratar al vecino como enemigo.

El domingo importa. Pero el lunes importa más.

A lo mejor un día, lejos, alguien se postule que no me haga sentir que estoy escogiendo entre dos males distintos.

Day 13/100 of #100DayswithTVS

The number that decides if you can afford your dream home.
Not your salary.
Not your credit score.
Not even the property price.
One number. Set by 6 people. In a room you’ll never enter.

Imagine this.
	2021.	Post-COVID euphoria. Interest rates are at historic lows. The RBI has flooded the economy with cheap money to keep India from falling apart during the pandemic.
A young couple in Pune both working, both saving decide this is the moment. They take a ₹50 lakh home loan at 6.5%. EMI: ₹33,000 a month. Tight, but doable. They sign the papers. They move in.
Life is good.

Then 2022 happens.
Inflation explodes globally. Oil prices surge. Russia invades Ukraine. Supply chains snap. In India, retail inflation hits 7.8% the highest in 8 years.
The RBI has one job in moments like this.
Cool it down.
And the fastest way to do that? Make money expensive.
Between May 2022 and February 2023, the RBI hiked the repo rate 6 times.
4% → 6.5%.
250 basis points. In 9 months.

EMI quietly climbed to ₹39,000.
₹6,000 more. Every single month. From a decision made in a building they’ve never visited, by people whose names they’ll never know.

So what is the repo rate?
Banks need money too. When they’re short, they borrow from the RBIndia’s central bank, the banker of all banks. The repo rate is the interest the RBI charges on that loan.
When repo rate goes up → borrowing costs more for banks → banks charge more from you → your home loan, car loan, business loan gets expensive.
When repo rate goes down → banks borrow cheap → they pass it on → EMIs fall, spending rises, economy breathes.
It’s a dial. The RBI turns it up to fight inflation. Turns it down to fight slowdown.
Simple in theory.
Brutal in practice if you’re on the wrong side of the cycle.

Here’s what makes it fascinating.
The RBI isn’t just looking at India when it sets the rate. It’s watching the US Fed. Oil prices. Monsoon forecasts. Global capital flows. The rupee. Inflation expectations six months from now.
6 people. Staring at the entire world. Deciding what your EMI will be next month.
And they can’t make everyone happy. Ever.
Lower rates → borrowers win, savers lose, inflation risks rise.
Higher rates → inflation cools, but growth slows, and the family that just bought a home starts skipping dinners out.
Every rate decision is a trade-off. Someone always pays.

The RBI held rates at 6.5% through all of 2023 and most of 2024. Then, in early 2025, as inflation finally eased, it began cutting.

Monetary policy doesn’t make headlines the way a scam does or a budget does.
But it quietly shapes whether you can afford a home, whether a startup can take a loan, whether a farmer can borrow before the harvest.

So the next time your bank sends you that EMI revision notice you’ll know exactly which room it came from.

Codex builds it. Claude Code reviews it. Hermes Agent verifies that neither of them is lying 🤯

Because here's the thing nobody tells you: your coding agent will say the build passes when it never ran the build. It'll say tests pass when it wrote tests that never executed.

So I made a cheat sheet for the one command that fixes that: /goal

A normal prompt asks for the next response. You read it, decide if it's right, push it forward. You steer every turn.

Goal flips that. You write down what "done" means. Tests pass, build passes, git status clean. You submit it once and the agent works toward exactly that until it's achieved, blocked, cleared, or out of budget.

But writing the goal isn't what makes it safe. The verifier is.

Hermes Agent, the orchestrator I run on a Mac Mini, never trusts a worker's self-report. After Codex marks a build done, Hermes runs the tests and the build itself before it believes a word of it. If you can't verify it from a shell, it isn't done.

That one rule turns /goal from a fancier prompt into a contract.

The cheat sheet below breaks down the rest:
• The anatomy of a good /goal and the four parts every one needs
• Who receives a /goal, and the one you actually write yourself
• Anti-patterns like "make it better," and what to write instead
• The verifier checklist for catching an agent that fakes a PASS

Codex, Claude Code, and Hermes. Three different teams, same primitive.

Workers change. The primitive stays the same.

Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4.8 today, while casually raising a new Series H round at nearly a $1T valuation! Alongside it, they also shipped Dynamic Workflows in Claude Code. The pitch: for the kind of tasks too big for one agent in one pass, Claude writes a Javascript orchestration script that fans the work out across hundreds of parallel subagents, has other agents try to refute the findings, and iterates until the answers converge.

The pattern underneath this is one others in the industry have been pointing at for a while now - deterministic orchestration around small, focused and optimized agent loops works much better than throwing a bunch of agents at a problem and hoping they figure out how to coordinate. The orchestration script is the backbone, the agents handle the work.

This took me back to a project we built at the LlamaIndex RAG-a-thon in October 2024, called Timeline of You, which was one of the first deep research approaches in the industry, before the category had a name. A few friends and I ended up winning the hackathon with it. Jay R. Abhinav Balasubramanian Aaditya Shukla Amala Deshmukh and Ashwani Agarwal!

Our pipeline leveraged specialized agents for different types of search, multimodal understanding, and document parsing. We used a knowledge graph as the shared source of information. The orchestration sits in deterministic code, the graph holds external context, and the agents stay focused on their slice.

That last bit also lines up with the Recursive Language Models work out of MIT (Alex Zhang et al.) that got a lot of attention since the end of last year. The core idea there is that instead of stuffing everything into the model's context window, the LLM writes Python code that manages an external context variable in a REPL and delegates work to sub-LLM calls. Same intuition here, the context goes outside the model, orchestration goes into code and focused sub-calls handle the actual work.

It's so exciting to see this pattern keep getting reinforced over the last 18 months: Gemini Deep Research (Dec 2024), OpenAI Deep Research (Feb 2025), Anthropic Research (Apr 2025), RLM (Dec 2025), and now Dynamic Workflows! 

Devpost blog, RLM paper, and the Anthropic launch post all in the comments!

India’s oil challenge is bigger than just fuel prices.

When crude oil becomes expensive the impact does not stay limited to petrol pumps. It moves through transport costs logistics food prices company margins, inflation, the rupee and even growth.

That is why oil is such a critical macro variable for India.

India imports a large share of its crude oil because domestic supply is not enough to meet demand. And since oil is bought in dollars a rise in global prices directly increases the import bill. 

In simple terms, more dollars leave the country the trade balance gets stressed and pressure builds on the rupee.

The real shock is how widely this spreads.

Higher oil prices increase truck and shipping costs. Businesses then pass those costs to consumers. That is how something as global as crude oil eventually shows up in daily essentials like food, packaged goods and household expenses.

This is also why RBI and policymakers track crude so closely. It can influence inflation current account deficit, interest rates and overall economic growth.

The big takeaway?
Oil is not just an energy input. It is a core economic input.
And when oil prices rise the effect does not remain isolated. It hits almost everything.

🔔 Your AI Isn’t Neutral. It’s Quietly Leaving People Out. That Risk Has a Name: Omissive Bias

Most enterprise leaders are auditing AI for what it says: hallucinations, toxicity, privacy failures, and discrimination. Few are auditing AI for what it leaves out. That blind spot is called omissive bias: the systematic under-inclusion of relevant moral, cultural, or religious perspectives in model outputs where a reasonable user would expect them to be considered.

As an AI auditor, I would not classify omissive bias as a cognitive bias. I would classify it as an AI governance and representational fairness risk.
Why? Because conversational AI is no longer a side tool. It is shaping customer service, employee guidance, care navigation, coaching, education, and other high-impact decisions. If a system repeatedly defaults to one narrow frame of reasoning while omitting perspectives that matter to real users, that is not neutrality. It is a coverage failure with business consequences.

A model can pass traditional tests for safety and still fail people by being systematically incomplete. That creates trust gaps, uneven user outcomes, adoption resistance, and reputational risk. In some sectors, it can also create compliance exposure when organizations claim fairness, inclusion, or responsible AI oversight without testing for viewpoint underrepresentation.

📣 Enterprise leaders should act now. Add omission checks to AI assurance programs. Benchmark ethically meaningful use cases. Test whether systems surface a reasonable range of relevant perspectives. Broken trust.

→ Communication becomes transparent
→ Friction disappears

When trust breaks:

Trust doesn't die in one big event.
It erodes quietly through small leadership missteps.

Saying one thing, doing another.
Values mean nothing if leaders don't mirror them daily.

Taking credit for team wins.
Great leaders shine the spotlight on their team, not themselves.

Hiding bad company news.
Teams can handle hard truths, just not being kept in the dark.

Deflecting blame during a crisis.
True leaders absorb responsibility, not pass it downward.

The most well-meaning parents can unknowingly pass on a habit that does more harm than good. Simply because nobody showed them a different way.

That habit is 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻.

Someone scored higher.
Someone performed better.
Someone reached a milestone faster.

In the moment, it may sound like motivation. But it teaches a child that success means becoming better than someone else.

The benchmark we set for our children influences how they see themselves for years.

What if the questions at home sounded different?

“Are you improving from where you were before?”
“Do you understand something today that confused you a few months ago?”
“Are you handling situations better than you did last year?”
“Did you push yourself a little further this time?”

When children begin measuring themselves against their own growth, something changes.

Other people stop looking like competition.
They start looking like people they can learn from.

That is when curiosity slowly replaces anxiety.

As parents, we have the opportunity to introduce a different conversation at home. One where confidence comes from growth, effort and progress rather than someone else’s report card.

The world our children are growing into may not remember who topped every class. But it will always value people who kept learning, adapting and raising their own standards.

Here's why some ductile iron castings survive a million cycles while others fail long before expected life...


Nodularity decides everything.

A casting can pass dimensional inspection, meet hardness requirements, and still crack under real world loading because the microstructure was never truly under control.

When graphite nodularity drops below 80 percent, elongation disappears and shock resistance collapses. What looks stable on paper quickly becomes a failure in the field.

That is why we treat magnesium timing as a process discipline, not a production adjustment.

Consistency in ductile iron is not created during inspection.
It is created during melting.

Base sulfur is another hidden variable that quietly destroys spherical graphite formation when it is not precisely controlled. Even small deviations can change the entire mechanical behavior of the casting.

This is why microstructural verification matters for every single heat.
Without it, you are not buying engineered components.

You are buying uncertainty.

The difference between long service life and premature failure is often invisible to the naked eye, but completely visible under metallurgical analysis.

The most expensive mistake in acquisitions is not a bad deal. It is the six months you spent chasing one that never fit.

I closed 58 acquisitions across three companies and worked with 9 private equity sponsors. Every one of those sponsors asked the same first question before we pursued a single target: what is your buy box?

A buy box is a one-page set of criteria that defines exactly what you are hunting before you start hunting. Revenue range. Geography. Margin profile. Customer concentration limits. Cultural fit markers. It fits on a single page.

That single page killed more bad deals than any advisor I ever hired.

Without it, founders burn months on diligence for targets that were never going to close. Legal fees stack. Teams lose focus. Opportunity cost compounds quietly in the background.

With it, every inbound opportunity gets a 15-minute filter. Pass or pursue. No gray area.

Discipline is not the opposite of speed. It is what makes speed possible.

I built the buy box framework into Empire Builder Academy because it is the first tool any acquisition-minded founder needs and the last one most of them build.

I built a model that grades every NFL fourth-down decision over the last 16 seasons against what the math actually says.

On every 4th down a coach can go for it, kick, or punt. My Expected Points model calculates the value of each option, picks the optimal one, and measures how many points the coach left on the table by choosing differently.

61,000 fourth downs later (2010–2025), here's what stood out:
→ The analytics revolution is real and measurable. Go-for-it rate nearly doubled (14.7% → 27.1%) while expected points lost per decision dropped ~30% league-wide.
→ Aggression and quality aren't the same thing. Some teams go for it a lot — in the wrong spots. The interesting ones pick the right moments.
→ The math is still bolder than the league on short yardage. The model and coaches agree 75% of the time, and most of the disagreement is on 4th-and-1.
→ The punt is the last great inefficiency. Coaches still punt more often than optimal.

The biggest lesson wasn't technical — it was learning to trust the football over the code. A few times the model spit out calls that didn't pass the smell test (going for it from your own 5, kicking field goals from 55 yards), and chasing down WHY was where the real learning happened.

Feedback is the most economic leadership tool we have. It is also the one  leaders tend to ration.

We tell ourselves we are being kind by waiting. The right moment. The right framing. The next 1:1 or an upcoming performance review. By the time the feedback arrives, the person has been operating on bad information for weeks. Sometimes months. That's not kindness. It's a tax we pass to the person who trusted us to help them grow.

Kim Scott named the pattern in Radical Candor. Care personally, challenge directly. Two things at once. The care is what gives you the right to challenge. The challenge is what proves the care was real.

Many managers I've coached are fluent in one and avoidant of the other. The warm ones soften the signal until it disappears. The direct ones forget that the relationship is the container the feedback lives inside. Both styles produce the same outcome. A pattern or habit that persists without integration. Team members adjusting around it. Trust erodes quietly.

A few things I have come to believe:
1. Feedback delayed is feedback distorted. The further you get from the moment, the more both of you have to reconstruct.
2. Specificity is a form of respect. Vague praise and vague criticism land the same way, which is to say they do not land.
3. The hard conversation is the work. Not the thing you do before the work, or after it. It is the work.

Most “AI agents” don’t get smarter over time.

They get fatter.

Every fix becomes another rule. Every edge case becomes another paragraph. Every “remember to...” gets bolted on until the thing is a 4,000-line instruction file that contradicts itself and still can’t do the job.

That’s not memory.

That’s hoarding.

I kept watching people, myself included, build skills and agents the same broken way:

→ stuffing instructions with things the model already knows  
→ writing one rule per scenario instead of one principle that covers many  
→ letting memory grow append-only until signal gets buried  
→ loading every bit of context every time, “just in case”

So I built a framework to stop it.

I call it APA: Adaptive Persistent Agent.

The idea is simple, but strict:

A good agent is not the one that remembers the most.

It’s the one that compresses the hardest.

APA splits an agent into four clean layers:

Instruction.  
Memory.  
Examples.  
Reflection.

Then every line has to pass one filter:

Does this earn its place, or is it baseline behavior dressed up as insight?

APA has two modes:

🔎 Audit mode scores an existing skill or workflow against 7 design signals and tells you the single highest-cost thing to fix first.

🛠️ Build mode scaffolds a new one that starts lean and learns through use instead of being over-configured upfront.

The goal is simple:

Agents that get sharper as they run, not heavier.

I’m giving it away for free. No course, no waitlist.

But I’d rather hand it to people who actually want to use it than spray a repo link into the void.

Great cooking isn't just about recipes—it's about mastering the techniques that transform ingredients into exceptional dishes.

Here are some essential culinary terms that every aspiring chef and food professional should understand:

🔹 Mise en Place – Everything in its place; ingredients prepped, measured, and ready before cooking begins.

🔹 Blanch – Briefly cook food in boiling water, then shock it in ice water to preserve color, texture, and nutrients.

🔹 Glaze – Apply a thin, glossy coating of sauce, stock reduction, or syrup to enhance flavor and presentation.

🔹 Sauté – Cook ingredients quickly in a small amount of fat over medium-high heat while stirring frequently.

🔹 Sift – Pass dry ingredients through a sieve to remove lumps and incorporate air for a lighter texture.

🔹 Emulsify – Combine two liquids that normally don't mix, such as oil and water, into a smooth and stable mixture.

🔹 Nappé – A classic test of sauce consistency; when a sauce coats the back of a spoon and leaves a clean line when drawn through.

🔹 Julienne – Cut vegetables into thin matchstick-shaped strips for precision and uniform cooking.

🔹 Brunoise – A fine dice created from julienned vegetables, commonly used in sauces, soups, and garnishes.

The difference between a cook and a culinary professional often lies in the mastery of these foundational techniques. These skills improve consistency, efficiency, presentation, and ultimately the guest experience.

In professional kitchens, excellence is built on fundamentals. Before creativity comes technique. Before innovation comes discipline.

Every perfectly plated dish begins with mastering the basics. 👌✨

As artificial intelligence becomes deeply embedded in academia, a troubling question continues to emerge:

Can AI detection tools reliably distinguish between human and AI-generated writing?

The evidence suggests the answer is far from clear.

Many universities, publishers, and researchers have raised concerns about the reliability of AI detection systems. Studies have shown that these tools can produce both false positives and false negatives. In other words, genuinely human-written work may be incorrectly flagged as AI-generated, while AI-generated content may pass through undetected (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023).

Imagine spending months conducting research, writing a paper from your own knowledge and experience, only to have a software tool wrongly label your work as AI-generated. Equally concerning is the possibility that heavily AI-generated content may escape detection altogether.

This raises important questions about academic integrity, fairness, due process, and the role of technology in evaluating scholarly work.

The way forward is not to rely solely on AI detectors as judges of academic misconduct. Instead, institutions should focus on:
✅ Process-based assessment
✅ Draft and revision histories
✅ Source verification and citation quality
✅ Oral defenses and presentations
✅ Critical thinking and originality of analysis

Technology should support academic integrity, not replace human judgment.

As educators, researchers, and students, we must ensure that the pursuit of integrity does not come at the expense of fairness.

Mastering Java Servlets: The RequestDispatcher Explained
Ever wondered how Java web applications seamlessly pass control from one component to another behind the scenes without the user ever noticing?

Enter the RequestDispatcher interface—the ultimate traffic cop of the Servlet container! 🚦

When building Java web applications, you often need to collaborate between different Servlets, JSPs, or HTML pages. The RequestDispatcher gives you the mechanism to do exactly that on the server side.

Here is a quick breakdown of its two superpowers:

1️⃣ The forward() Method (The Complete Handoff) 🔄
How it works: Servlet A processes a portion of the request and completely passes the torch to Servlet B. Servlet B is solely responsible for sending the final response to the client.

Real-World Example: A user submits a login form to LoginServlet. If credentials match, the servlet forwards the request to dashboard.jsp. The URL in the browser still says /LoginServlet, but the user safely sees their dashboard!

2️⃣ The include() Method (The Layout Builder) 🧱
How it works: Servlet A retains control but pulls in the content or layout from another resource (like a banner, footer, or sidebar) right into its own response.

Real-World Example: Building a consistent web page layout. Your main content servlet includes header.jsp at the top and footer.jsp at the bottom to assemble a fully formed page before sending it to the client.

💡 Key Takeaway for Developers:
Both forward() and include() happen entirely on the server side. Because the browser is kept in the dark about this internal routing, the URL in the address bar never changes.

(This is completely different from response.sendRedirect(), which forces the browser to make a brand-new HTTP request!)

🏫 Primary Key is your Student ID. Foreign Key is your Enrollment Form.

For Example. 

📌 Primary Key = Character ID Card 🪪  
→ Every CHARACTER gets ONE unique ID  
→ No duplicate IDs allowed  
→ Cannot be NULL  
→ Identifies each character uniquely  

🎮 CREATE TABLE friends (
      friend_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
      name VARCHAR(100));

📌 Foreign Key = Apartment Entry Pass ☕🚪  
→ The pass contains the Friend’s ID  
→ Connects a friend to apartments, cafes, or events  
→ Invalid Friend ID = entry rejected ❌  
→ One friend can appear in many places  

🎮 CREATE TABLE hangouts (
      hangout_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
      friend_id INT REFERENCES friends(friend_id),
      location VARCHAR(100));

When relationships break ⛓️‍💥

→ Fake friend ID in hangouts = orphan record  

→ Deleting a friend without handling hangouts = ghost data 👻  

→ App UI may show no hangouts while DB still has records

  

Main SQL Checklist ✅

→ Are Friend IDs still unique after bulk inserts?  

→ Does every hangout point to a real friend?  

→ What happens to hangouts when a friend is deleted?  

→ Are foreign key constraints properly enforced?  


No valid Friend ID = No valid Hangout.  
No valid Primary Key = No valid Foreign Key. 🔑

🚨 Interview Question That Confuses Even Experienced Developers 👀
“Access Token vs Refresh Token in Salesforce — Explain Like You’re in a Real Interview.”
Here’s the easiest way to remember it 👇
🔑 Access Token
Short-lived token
Used to access Salesforce APIs/resources
Sent in every API request
Expires quickly for security
Think of it like:
 🎟️ A temporary visitor pass to enter a building
Example:
 You call Salesforce REST API → Access Token validates your request.
🔄 Refresh Token
Long-lived token
Used to generate a NEW Access Token
Not sent in every request
Improves user experience by avoiding repeated logins
Think of it like:
 🪪 Your ID card used to get a new visitor pass
🔥 Real Interview Twist:
👉 “Why not use Refresh Token directly for API calls?”
Because Refresh Tokens are HIGHLY sensitive.
 If compromised, attackers can continuously generate new Access Tokens.
That’s why:
 ✅ Access Tokens = frequent usage
 ✅ Refresh Tokens = secure storage only
💡 Best Practice in Salesforce Integrations:
Store Refresh Tokens securely
Use OAuth 2.0 flows properly
Never expose tokens in frontend code
Rotate/revoke tokens when needed
🧠 One-Line Answer for Interviews:
“Access Token gives temporary API access, while Refresh Token helps generate new Access Tokens without asking the user to log in again.”

I loved the law, but I didn't love the law firm lifestyle. Firm Prospect's recent report on lateral hiring shows I was not alone in that. Attorneys today are looking for more sustainable options. 

Over the last five years, the rate at which AmLaw associates are leaving for boutique firms has almost doubled. Honestly, it makes total sense. We are in the era of employees demanding more from their employers. Here are a few reasons why downsizing the firm can have a big upside to your career: 

1. Better substantive experience. I talk to attorneys all day, every day - and this is probably the top reason AmLaw litigation associates specifically tend to move. No one wants to be an 8th year litigation associate who has never litigated. When teams are lean, you get more hands-on experience, and you get it quickly. 

2. Better work-life harmony. Top 50 firms typically have a stated billable requirement of 1900-2000 hours. Even with firms that have "no requirement", associates tend to crank out significantly more. There are a number of reasons for this but to name a few: bonus potential, partnership potential, fear of the up-or-out model, even internal pressure because these folks did not make it to the top by being content with the minimum. The burnout rate in this field is extremely high, and when you've been billing at an unsustainable pace, billing a thousand hours less annually starts to sound extremely appealing. 

3. The work and clients are still extremely sophisticated. Need some evidence? Check the Chambers rankings. You'll probably be surprised how many smaller firms are listed alongside household names. How are they punching above their weight? Most of these powerhouse boutiques are started by former AmLaw partners who wanted more control to run their practice, their way, at a pace that works for them, and their clients are going with.

4. Comp is still competitive. Most of them are not paying market, but it's worth pointing out that some do, and highly specialized boutiques may even pay above market. What is really changing though, are associates' perspectives. More and more frequently I am hearing, "I don't consider it a step back if the hours are proportionate." Especially when you consider the long game which brings me to number 5...

5. More attainable & customized path to partnership. Smaller firms are generally hiring with the intention that you will become partner. They are also much more flexible - some don't have class years, or even a hard-and-fast rule of required tenure. Particularly at firms with two tiers of partnership, associates may even move vertically instead of laterally -  pass go, collect $200 dollars, and go straight to partner without a book of business.

Anneal is a machine learning compiler written in Go. Not a tensor library. Not an autodiff wrapper. A real graph-rewrite compiler that trains neural nets on Metal GPU.

Heavily inspired by tinygrad, which treats everything, including gradients, as passes over an immutable intermediate representation. I wanted to understand that architecture deeply enough to build it from scratch.

A few things worth calling out:

Gradients are a rewrite pass over the same graph as the forward pass. This lets the compiler fuse kernels across the forward/backward boundary, something you give up with a more traditional autodiff approach.

The rewrite driver is iterative rather than recursive. tinygrad's is recursive, which risks stack exhaustion on deep graphs. Anneal sidesteps that.

The backend targets WebGPU, running on Metal, through zero-CGO Go bindings.

It trains MLPs and conv nets end to end. There is still a lot left to build, and tinygrad's codebase keeps teaching me things.

The repo is open if you want to dig in.

AI gave us more code than we can review. It also gave us a glut of posts about reviewing code. 

This is one of those posts. I'll keep it short.

Code review was always doing several jobs at once. It spread knowledge and norms. It caught bugs. It checked that the right thing got built, and that it got built right. We lumped them together because one person did them all in a single pass. Pulling them apart is what makes the load easier to shed.

Knowledge and norms. LLMs can't follow them unless they can read them. Documenting these used to be the chore nobody did. Voice transcription and a model to tidy up the result have made it cheap enough to actually happen. Bonus points if we're updating docs from MR comments.

Bugs and rules. Anything that reduces to pass or fail should be a test, not a person. I used to skim the MR by hand looking for common issues. Writing a script to enforce each one cost more than the bug it caught, so I never did. Now writing the script takes less time than skimming the MR. No reaching across a boundary. No monkey-patching. These are tests now, not opinions in a review thread.

The right thing. The code can behave exactly as specified and still be wrong. Statisticians call that a Type III error, the right answer to the wrong question. No test catches it, because the test would have to know what you meant. So the judgment stays with the person. You can still automate the evidence it needs. A short video of the feature running. A diagram showing what moved and what it touches. Deliver the reviewer to the decision instead of making them hunt for it.

HOW DO RETRIES AFFECT NETWORK ASSERTIONS?  

Retry mechanisms can lead to false positives by masking intermittent failures and network issues.  

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE:  
- Inconsistent test outcomes.  
- Flaky tests with variable results.  
- Tests pass despite network disturbances.  
- Harder to debug real network problems.  

ROOT CAUSES:  
- Over-reliance on retry logic.  
- Undetected network timeouts.  
- Hidden server responses.  
- Cascading assertion failures.  
- Misconfigured retry intervals.  

WHY THIS IS DANGEROUS:  
- Creates a misleading test report.  
- Hides potential performance issues.  
- Leads to unreliable software releases.  
- Impacts user experience negatively.  

WHY IT GOES UNNOTICED:  
Retries mask issues by passing tests that should fail, leading to false security in test results.  

CORRECT DESIGN:  
- Limit retries to critical cases.  
- Log both successful and failed retries.  
- Regularly review retry configurations.  
- Ensure visibility into retry outcomes.  
- Monitor for network performance variances.  

SIMPLE RULE:  
Don't let retries turn a blind eye toward underlying issues.  

HARD QUESTION:  
Are retries making your tests pass or just making problems invisible?

My career has taken some interesting turns. Like the time I helped fight for an elephant's human rights.

A few years ago, I worked with the Nonhuman Rights Project on one of the most remarkable things I've ever been a part of as a communicator — building awareness and grassroots support for the first-of-its-kind legal fight for Happy, an Asian elephant who lived in solitude at the Bronx Zoo, to be recognized as a person entitled to the fundamental right to bodily liberty.

The argument was simple and radical at once: that an elephant of Happy's cognitive complexity (she was the first elephant to “pass” the mirror self-recognition test), deserved more than a life spent alone in a one-acre prison. If the court had ruled in her favor, she would have been transferred to a sanctuary.

Despite a strong case that The Atlantic called "the most important animal-rights case of the 21st century" — and support from leading legal scholars, including Laurence Tribe — the court ruled against her. Happy remained captive at the Bronx Zoo for the rest of her life and yesterday, she was euthanized. 

I keep thinking about what it meant that this case was argued at all — that a serious legal team stood before a court and made the case for an elephant's rights, and that the court had to genuinely grapple with it. The law didn't catch up in time for Happy, but I believe — I hope —  history will look back on this case as foundational. I'm proud to have played even a small role in it.

I don't have a clean takeaway. I'm just sad — for her, and for what could have been. Rest easy, Happy. You deserved so much more.
